question_en: An investor wants to price a two-year, 6% annual coupon bond. Spot rates are 5% for zero-coupon, one-year bonds of similar credit quality and 7% for similar, zero-coupon, two-year bonds. Based on this information, the price of the bond per 100 of par value is closest to:
explanation_en:
HP 12c TI BA II Plus
A coupon-paying bond can be conceptualized as a series of zero-coupon bonds. Each cash flow is identical to a zero-coupon bond that has a
face value equal to the cash flow and matures at the time of the payment. The present value (ie, price) of any zero-coupon bond is its face value
discounted by its spot rate.
This leads to the "no-arbitrage" rule for pricing bonds. Since any cash flow of a coupon-paying bond is economically equivalent to its
corresponding zero-coupon bond, both must have the same value. Any discrepancy allows an investor to realize riskless arbitrage profits. To
prevent arbitrage, each cash flow must be discounted at the same rate as for a zero-coupon bond of the same maturity (eg, the spot rate for that
maturity).
The sum of the present values for all cash flows is the "no-arbitrage" price of the bond. The calculations are shown below:
(Choice A) 98.19 is the present value from using 7% as the discount rate for both the bonds' cash flows.
(Choice C) 101.86 results from using 5% as the discount rate for both the bonds' cash flows.

question_en: An investor is considering a three-year investment and has calculated a "2y1y" forward rate of 2.75%. If a two-year zero-coupon bond's YTM is 1.85% and a three-year zero-coupon bond's YTM is 2.15%, the forward rate is best described as the:
option_a: implied spot rate of a two-year zero-coupon bond in one year.
option_b: required rate of return to invest in the three-year zero-coupon bond.
option_c: breakeven reinvestment rate on a one-year zero-coupon bond in two years.
explanation_en:
The implied forward rate (or just "forward rate") is an interest rate derived from the current zero-coupon bond term structure (ie, spot curve).
Arbitrage-free pricing enforces the consistency of forward rates with spot rate differences. A forward rate can be interpreted as the incremental
return required for extending the time-to-maturity by an additional period.
For example, in this scenario an investor would be indifferent to investing in a three-year zero-coupon bond at 2.15% or investing in a two-year
zero-coupon bond at 1.85% and then, two years from now, in a one-year zero-coupon bond at 2.75% (ie, the "2y1y" forward rate), since both result
in the same return in three years.
The implied forward rate is the breakeven reinvestment rate required to make the two transactions equivalent. If an investor believes that the
one-year rate two years in the future will be lower than the breakeven rate of 2.75%, the investor is better off buying the three-year zero-coupon
bond today.
(Choice A) The implied spot rate of a two-year zero-coupon bond in one year is quoted as 1y2y, not 2y1y.
(Choice B) The rate of return of the three-year zero-coupon bond is known (ie, 2.15%); it is the return of the one-year zero-coupon bond in two
years that is uncertain. The implied forward rate is the required rate of return for the investor to be indifferent to the two transactions.

question_en: Which of the following is most likely a valid assumption in constructing a par yield curve?
option_a: A par yield curve mainly uses bonds that are priced at par.
option_b: All cash flows from a bond are discounted at the same rate.
option_c: Each bond uses the same periodicity regardless of maturity.
explanation_en:
A par curve is constructed from a spot curve. Both curves discount cash flows by the spot rate for each period that the cash flow occurs;
therefore, the discounting rates for both curves assume the same periodicity across all maturities.
The main difference between the par and spot curves is that the present values of bonds included in a spot curve can differ from their par values.
The par curve assumes that each bond's present value always equals its par value. This assumption allows yields for different maturities to be
compared directly.
The par yield is the assumed coupon rate that makes the present value equal to the par value when discounting the cash flows using the spot
rates, as shown by the formula below:
As the table above demonstrates, the difference between the yield measures is not significant, being as small as one or two basis points in some
cases.
(Choice A) The par curve is derived from adjusting a bond's payments so that the present value is equal to the par value, but the actual market
price can be any value.
(Choice B) Each cash flow is discounted at the spot rate for the period when the cash flow occurs. Since spot rates can be (and usually are)
different for each maturity, cash flows are discounted at different rates.

question_en:
An investor replicates a 4-year, 2% annual coupon-paying Treasury bond with 100 par value by combining zero-coupon bonds with the following spot rates:

| Time to Maturity (years) | Spot Rates (annual) |
|---|---|
| 1 | 0.5% |
| 2 | 1.7% |
| 3 | 2.8% |
| 4 | 4.0% |

The YTM on the bond is closest to:
explanation_en:
A fixed-rate coupon Treasury bond can be replicated from a series of zero-coupon bonds (strips) with the same pattern of cash flows. The
price of the fixed-rate bond should equal the sum of the face values of the individual strips discounted by their corresponding spot rates (ie, the
market discount rate for zero-coupon bonds). This is known as the arbitrage-free valuation approach since the same price applies to both
instruments; otherwise, arbitrage opportunities will be present.
The YTM is the rate that discounts a bond's future cash flows to its current price. To calculate the YTM (r) of a fixed-rate bond, first calculate the
bond's present value (ie, price) using the cash flows of the zero-coupon strips, and then input the present value and other parameters (ie, maturity,
coupons, par value) on the calculator to solve for r.
(Choice A) 3.00% results from incorrectly using 8 (ie, assuming semiannual periods) for the number of periods.
(Choice C) 4.43% results from failing to include the last coupon payment of 20 in period 4's cash flow when computing the bond's present value.

question_en: The risk-free yields for a spot curve constructed from government debt instruments most likely refer to the absence of:
explanation_en:
A yield curve allows comparisons between yields of bonds over different maturities (ie, term structure of interest rates). Most yield curves are
based on government bonds, which have no risk of defaulting on principal or coupon payments. However, government bonds have different
coupon rates for different maturities, so each maturity reflects some degree of reinvestment risk. This risk can prevent accurate analysis of the
term structure.
The spot curve is the government bond yield curve constructed from a series of government zero-coupon bonds of different maturities. Zero-
coupon bonds do not pay periodic interest, so they have no reinvestment risk since there is nothing to reinvest until maturity. Although the spot
curve reflects the absence of both credit and reinvestment risks, it addresses neither liquidity risk nor inflation risk.
(Choice B) The demand for government bonds is not the same for all maturities. Bonds for which there is low demand can exhibit lack of liquidity,
posing liquidity risk. This would manifest as a higher spread between the bid and ask prices that dealers quote for the bonds.
(Choice C) Most government bonds do not adjust their coupon rates or principal to keep pace with inflation, so government bond yields do not
account for inflation risk.

subtopic: 7.10 Interest Rate Risk and Return
question_en: A coupon bond's Macaulay duration is most accurately described as the holding period over which:
option_a: the value of cash flows received equal the cost of buying the bond.
option_b: changes in reinvestment income offset changes in the bond's price.
option_c: the bond earns a risk-free return if hedged by shorting a government bond.
explanation_en: Noncallable coupon bonds contain two types of interest rate risk: reinvestment risk and price risk. Reinvestment risk dominates in the long run and price risk dominates in the short run. Logically, somewhere in between the short run and the long run, there should be a balance point. That point is the Macaulay duration: the holding period to the point where changes in reinvestment income and changes in price offset one another exactly. Interest rates increase: additional reinvestment income and bond price decreases Interest rates decrease: reduced reinvestment income and bond price increases No matter the direction, the impact of a rate change is positive for one source of return, but negative for the other. In the short run, price risk dominates. Interest rate changes affect bond prices immediately. In the long run, reinvestment risk dominates since its impact builds over time as more coupons are reinvested. A bond's Macaulay duration is the holding period over which those risks balance each other. (Choice A) Market price equals the present value of the coupon and principal, so a bond must be held to maturity to receive cash flows with a value equal to the cost of the bond. Since Macaulay duration is the present value weighted average time of the cash flows, a coupon bond's Macaulay duration is shorter than its time to maturity. (Choice C) Although it is a type of hedge, the strategy is not riskless and therefore does not lock in a risk-free rate of return.

question_en: Five years ago, an investor purchased a 10-year, 7% semiannual coupon paying bond for 98. Today the bond is sold for 98.25. The capital gain or loss per 100 of par value is closest to:
explanation_en: An investor's capital gain or loss equals the selling price minus the carrying value at the time of the sale. At any point in time, the bond's carrying value is the initial price adjusted for the accumulated amortization of the discount or premium. For a bond initially issued at a discount, carrying value increases over time until it reaches par value at maturity. For a bond initially issued at a premium, carrying value decreases over time until it reaches par value at maturity. In this question, the bond was initially purchased at a discount. To find the capital gain or loss: (Choice A) −1.75 capital loss results from subtracting the par value 100 from the sales price 98.25. (Choice C) 0.25 capital gain results from subtracting the initial price 98 from the sales price 98.25.

explanation_en: Macaulay duration is a type of yield duration that measures the sensitivity of a bond's full price to changes in its own YTM. The Macaulay duration is the weighted average time to receipt of the bond's payments. The weights are the portions of the bond's full price that correspond to each of the future payments. Macaulay duration can also be thought of as the average time to receipt of the bond's payments that will result in realization of the bond's initial, stated YTM. In this scenario: t/T = 0/T = 0 since the bond settles on its July 11, 2023 coupon payment date YTM is 10.2% and YTM per period is r = (0.102 / 2) = 0.051 Coupon per period is c = (0.07 / 2) = 0.035 N = 23 = (11.5 years × 2 semiannual periods per year) Substitute these values into the formula to calculate the bond's Macaulay duration per period: The result of this calculation is the bond's Macaulay duration per period. Dividing by the number of periods per year results in the bond's annual Macaulay duration: 15.18 ÷ 2 = 7.59. (Choice A) 7.1 is the result of incorrectly interpreting the fact that the bond's settlement is on the coupon payment date to mean that t = T, so that t/T = 1. The correct value of t/T in this question is 0/T = 0. (Choice C) 15.2 is the result of failing to convert Macaulay duration per period into annual Macaulay duration.

question_en: An investor with a 10-year investment horizon purchases a noncallable 10-year, 7% annual coupon bond. The bond purchase price is 107.360087 per 100 of par value, with a 6% YTM. The bond's annual modified duration is 7.180. The duration gap at the time of the investment is closest to:
explanation_en: A bond investor's rate of return is equal to the bond's YTM if: the issuer does not default, the bond is held until maturity, and the coupons are reinvested at the initial YTM. In this scenario, since the YTM on the identical bonds changes and the investors have different time horizons, the rates of return differ. A bond's annual rate of return is its annualized holding period return based on the sum of its reinvested coupons and its sale price: A change in YTM affects both the coupon reinvestment rate and the price of the bond prior to maturity. In this scenario, interest rates fall, negatively impacting the rate at which coupons can be reinvested. This disproportionately disadvantages Investor Y, who has a longer holding period (3 years) and redeems at par; therefore, Investor Y depends more on the coupon reinvestment portion of the return. Investor Y's rate of return (8.82%) is less than the bond's initial YTM (8.88%). Investor X, who sells the bond before maturity and therefore has a shorter holding period, is more affected by the bond's price than the rate of coupon reinvestment. Since interest rates decrease, the bond's price rises; therefore, Investor X is positively impacted. Investor X's rate of return (9.28%) is greater than the bond's initial YTM (8.88%). Investor X's rate of return is about 0.46% (9.28% − 8.82%) greater than Investor Y's rate of return (Choices A and B). question_en: An investor buys a newly issued 20-year bond at par. The bond pays a 6% annual coupon. Shortly after purchase, the bond's YTM falls to 5% and stays at that level until the bond is sold at the end of three years. If the reinvestment rate over the period is 5%, the investor's annualized rate of return over the three-year investment horizon is closest to:
explanation_en:
The rate of return (or horizon return) is the geometric average annual rate that equates the initial investment with the value accumulated by
the end of the holding period (ie, investment horizon). The accumulated value, or total money return, is the sum of:
price at which the bond is sold
cumulative coupon payments
reinvestment income on any coupons received before the end of the holding period
These three components can be computed in two steps. The bond must be priced at a 5% yield three years in the future (when 17 years remain
until maturity). The coupon payments plus reinvestment income are calculated simultaneously by solving for the future value of an annuity.
The total money return divided by the initial investment is equal to 1 + the total rate of return. That outcome is annualized by raising it to the power
of (1/holding period) and subtracting 1 (ie, removing the value of the initial investment).
(Choice A) 8.94% uses a total money return reflecting only the bond price and the three coupons received over the investment horizon. This
solution omits the reinvestment income on the first two coupons.
(Choice C) 10.06% is the arithmetic (rather than the standard geometric) average annual return. 10.06% is based on the accurate total rate of
return (30.19%) divided by 3, rather than (1 + total rate of return)1/3 – 1.

price at which the bond is sold
cumulative coupon payments
reinvestment income on any coupons received before the end of the holding period
Those three components can be calculated in two steps. The bond must be priced at an 8% YTM, 6 years in the future when 16 years (ie, 32
coupon periods) remain until maturity. The coupon payments plus reinvestment income are calculated simultaneously by solving for the future

The total money return divided by the initial investment equals 1 + the total rate of return. Annualize that outcome by raising it to the power of (1 /

question_en: A bond matures in 3 years and pays a 7% annual coupon. The bond is currently trading at 104.0469 per 100 par value with a 5.50% yield-to-maturity. The Macaulay duration of the bond is closest to:
explanation_en:
The Macaulay duration is a function of maturity, coupon, and yield. It is the weighted average time until the coupons and principal are due.
The timing of each payment is weighted by its present value as a percent of the bond's full price. Another way to calculate the Macaulay duration

(Choice A) 2.64 results from using only the par value for the final cash flow (ie, failing to include the last coupon).
(Choice C) 2.93 results from dividing the time weighted present value of the cash flows (the numerator in the calculation) by the par value of 100
rather than the market price of 104.0469.

question_en:
An investor purchases a bond for a price of 111.62. The bond is a 10-year callable bond with a 7% coupon paid annually. If the bond's benchmark yield curve shifts by 30 basis points and its YTM changes by 25 basis points, the bond's price is expected to be:

- 110.23 if interest rates rise, or
- 112.99 if interest rates fall.

Based on only this information and using the most appropriate measure of duration, the bond's duration is closest to:
explanation_en:
A bond's interest rate risk is measured by duration and convexity. Together, these two measurements are used to estimate the change in a bond's
price due to a given change in interest rates. Interest rate changes can be represented as changes in the bond's yield-to-maturity or shifts in a
benchmark yield curve.
An embedded call option creates uncertainty in a bond's cash flows and, therefore in its YTM, since the bond may be called (ie, redeemed) before
maturity. Thus, for a callable bond, it makes sense to estimate price changes based on a shift in the benchmark yield curve instead of the
YTM.
Approximate modified duration and convexity measure changes in a bond's price based on changes in its YTM.
Effective duration and convexity measure changes in a bond's price based on shifts in its benchmark yield curve.
In this scenario, since the bond is callable, interest rate changes are represented by a shift in the benchmark yield curve, and therefore effective
duration is appropriate. Substitute the bond price and benchmark rate change data into the formula to calculate effective duration:
(Choice B) 4.95 is the approximate modified duration of the bond. Approximate modified duration is not appropriate for use with callable bonds.
(Choice C) −19.91 is the effective convexity of the bond based on the given data, not the effective duration.
